fact_policy: Original factual annotations. Numeric facts retain units and locators; unknowns and authored routes are separate. No numerical plots were digitized.

facts.fact: Final 2011 Nature Communications research article; laboratory nonbiological glass-grain/water-glycerol/air experiments plus analytical modeling.

Two glass plates of 350 by 350 by 10 mm form a 200 by 300 by 0.5 mm channel with double-sided tape on three sides, inlet at one end and opposite end open. A similar 19 mm-thick-plate cell serves high-stiffness experiments.

Granules are polydisperse glass beads of average diameter 100 micrometres, mostly spherical with angular grains and smaller particles also present; no supplier or complete size/shape distribution is given.

The reported host is a 50% water/glycerol solution. Added glycerol keeps grains suspended during loading; they subsequently sediment on the lower plate. The percentage basis, stock purity and settling interval are not given.

The filling fraction phi is normalized to the close-packed-grain filling fraction. It is not identical to absolute glass volume fraction; Methods uses 0.6 as the solid volume fraction of close-packed spheres.

Air is driven from a syringe by an Aladdin/WPI pump. Pressure is sensed by HCL0075D/Sensor Technics with NI cDAQ9172 and NI9237. PL-B742U/Pixelink camera below the cell acquires time-lapse images, using a white screen and two high-frequency fluorescent lights for brightfield.

facts.fact: The paired low-rate examples use phi 0.23 and 0.58, air reservoir 30 ml and reported pump rate 0.02 ml/min. Lower phi yields a branched finger pattern; higher phi yields pronounced separate bubble bursts. Figure 2 supplies pressure, invaded-volume and derived-flow panels for selected numbered events.

The illustrated filling-fraction/reservoir sweep fixes q at 0.03 ml/min, with axis labels phi 0.23,0.35,0.46,0.58,0.69 and Vair 3.75,7.5,15,30,60,120 ml. Some intersections are blank; the image is not evidence of a complete factorial set. Independent visual audit counted 22 displayed examples, not 30 factorial combinations; this does not establish the total number of runs performed.

Finger width is measured as 2A/S, where A is invaded area and S interface length. Bubble-volume distributions at phi 0.58 are shown for reservoir labels 7.5,15,30,60,120 ml. Distribution widths and medians increase with reservoir; individual bubble events vary substantially.

Morphology measures include S/A and adjacent maximum/minimum width ratio. Standard-deviation bars on two S/A points come from replicate experiments, but the replicate count is not stated. Width-ratio means and standard deviations use 20 random measurements; they are not 20 independent preparations.

The finger/bubble model uses effective mu 0.53 and kappa 0.8 fitted to the width observations. A plus/minus10% mu envelope is shown for the phase boundary; it is a parameter sensitivity illustration, not a confidence interval.

At phi 0.58 and Vair 30 ml, rate variation spans four decades. Reported behavior progresses from frictional events to partially fluidized/coral fronts and then suspension/viscous fingering. The full numerical run schedule is not supplied as a table.

The predicted 0.05 ml/min rate is a lower bound for possible continuous motion, not an empirical transition threshold. Main text places observed crossover above 0.1 ml/min, describes intermittency at 0.3, fluidized-front behavior over 0.3-3, coral examples at 1, and re-suspension beyond approximately 10 with branched fingers at 30 ml/min.
The written movie description labels coral growth0.1 ml/min, whereas the movie intro/summary and coral panels say 1.0 ml/min, matching main p 5. This discrepancy remains flagged.

A reported control decreases injection rate by a factor 100 and increases viscosity by the same factor, obtaining the same coral pattern and supporting inverse-viscosity rate scaling. The altered fluid recipe, absolute starting/ending pair and repeats are not provided.

Increasing phi produces a reported fracturing regime at approximately phi greater than0.9 in deformable granular material. This means granular-pattern fracture, not intentional breaking of the glass plates. Fine preparation, loads and run schedule are unspecified.

Close-packed porous-medium capillary/viscous illustrations in Figure 5 derive from other authors and experimental setups (references 38 and 42); they are contextual comparisons, not new measurements from this paper. The extended diagram and phase lines are tentative guides.
Figure 5 organizes phi inverse (phi^-1), rate and stiffness. Grain roughness, host viscosity and density contrast can shift boundaries; the schematic is not a calibrated universal classifier.

The analytical treatment uses isothermal ideal-gas compliance, K=P0/Vair, and adds a roughly 240 Pa out-of-plane capillary contribution to the background pressure. The p 7 printed intermediate Boyle-law relation has an apparent sign inconsistency with the expansion narrative and negative pressure-drop approximation; no correction is applied here.

Reported modeling parameters include glass density 2400 kg/m3, fluid density 1130 kg/m3, close-packed porosity 0.4, gap 0.5 mm, viscosity 0.01 Pa s and observed bubble radius around 3 cm. These are model context rather than new qualification limits.

Data and image analyses used unspecified standard commercial software. Camera/DAQ synchronization, exposure, sampling rates, calibration uncertainty, segmentation algorithm and absolute raw recordings are not provided.

The final paper has five numbered figures and nine equations, no numbered scientific tables; the associated supplementary inventory has two movies and their written descriptions. Separate raw data or source code is not listed in the reviewed record.
